title: Build the Playwright E2E suite for chart interaction, multi-pane and sync
body:
## Context
`03-testing-strategy.md` places E2E at the top of the pyramid: few tests, high value, covering the paths that only exist when everything is assembled. For the chart engine that means the interaction paths — a real pointer dragging a real canvas in a real browser, with a real worker decoding real frames — which is precisely where the unit tests' assumptions get tested.

This suite also covers **multi-pane and cross-chart sync** (E11-S09, CMP-196), which is untestable at any lower level: sync is a property of several chart instances interacting through a shared worker, and a unit test of the propagation function cannot tell you whether two charts actually stay aligned.

The suite runs in **both web and Electron**, since Electron is the primary shell and has its own process model.

## Scope / Deliverables
- Playwright suite in `packages/chart-engine/test/e2e` (and the `apps/web` harness route it drives), running against **Chromium** and **Electron**.
- **Interaction**: drag-to-pan; wheel zoom at cursor with the anchored-point invariant asserted; `Shift+wheel` horizontal pan; `Ctrl+wheel` price zoom; time-axis drag to compress/expand; double-click reset; momentum settling; pinch-zoom via synthesised touch.
- **Keyboard**: full keyboard-only traversal — focus the chart, step the data cursor, rescale both axes, reset, open the table with `Alt+T` — with **no pointer events dispatched at all** in those specs, so a regression that makes something pointer-only fails the suite.
- **Scales**: each mode via the SCR-043 menu, autoscale engage/disengage, lock badge appearance, double-click restore, and the log-unavailable case.
- **Crosshair**: pointer and keyboard movement, readout values asserted against fixture data, countdown display and its warn state, magnet behaviour.
- **Multi-pane** (E11-S09): pane stacking, splitter drag **and keyboard resize**, collapse/restore, height-ratio persistence.
- **Sync groups** (CMP-196): time-range, crosshair and price-level sync across 2–4 panes and across 2 chart instances; assertion that propagation happens **exactly once per group per frame** and that a subscriber applying a sync does not re-publish.
- **Cross-instance**: the SCR-049 multi-chart grid case with 4 charts sharing one worker.
- Fixture-driven with a **fake WS server** replaying a recorded session, so tests are deterministic and hermetic.
- Flake controls: no arbitrary sleeps (wait on engine-emitted events), deterministic virtual clock where possible, and a quarantine lane with a mandatory ticket for anything that flakes.

## Out of scope
- Perf measurement — **E11-Q03** (E2E timings are too noisy to gate on).
- Accessibility conformance — **E11-Q05** (this suite asserts keyboard *functionality*, not WCAG conformance).
- Chaos scenarios — **E11-Q04**.
- Series, indicator, drawing and footprint behaviour — those Epics' own E2E additions, which extend this harness.

## Acceptance criteria
```gherkin
Scenario: The keyboard-only specs dispatch no pointer events
  Given the keyboard traversal specs
  When they execute
  Then no pointer, mouse or touch event is dispatched anywhere in those specs
  And every assertion still passes, proving the paths are genuinely keyboard-operable

Scenario: Cursor-anchored zoom holds its invariant under real input
  Given the pointer is over the bar at a known timestamp
  When the wheel is scrolled to zoom in and then back out
  Then that timestamp remains under the cursor throughout, within one pixel
  And the assertion is made on the rendered viewport, not on an internal call

Scenario: Sync propagates exactly once per frame
  Given four charts in one sync group
  When the crosshair moves on chart 1
  Then charts 2, 3 and 4 update in the same frame
  And an instrumentation counter confirms exactly one propagation per group per frame, with no echo

Scenario: The suite runs in both Chromium and Electron
  When the suite executes in CI
  Then every spec runs in both runtimes
  And an Electron-only failure is reported as such rather than being hidden behind a Chromium pass

Scenario: The suite is deterministic
  Given the same commit and the same fixture
  When the suite runs ten times
  Then it passes ten times
  And any spec that does not is quarantined with a ticket rather than retried silently

Scenario: Splitters are operable by keyboard
  Given a pane splitter has focus
  When arrow keys are pressed
  Then the pane ratio changes by the specified step and the new value is announced
  And the same end state is reachable as by dragging
```

## Technical notes / design
**Waiting on events, not on time.** The engine emits `viewport`, `frame` and `pick` messages; the harness exposes them on `window.__engineEvents` so specs await a real state change rather than `waitForTimeout`. Arbitrary sleeps are the primary cause of flaky rendering tests and are banned in this suite by lint rule, not by convention.

**Synthesising gestures.** Playwright's `mouse.wheel` and `touchscreen` APIs cover wheel and pinch; momentum requires dispatching a pointer sequence with realistic timestamps, so the harness provides a `flick(dx, dy, durationMs)` helper that produces a physically plausible velocity — a flick synthesised as two events a frame apart produces an absurd velocity and tests nothing real.

**Electron specifics.** The Electron runner uses `_electron.launch` against the built app; the worker and OffscreenCanvas paths differ subtly from the browser (different process model, different GPU process behaviour), which is exactly why both runtimes are required rather than assumed equivalent.

**Sync assertion.** Propagation counting uses the `engine.sync.propagations_per_frame` counter from E11-S09 — an assertion on observable instrumentation rather than on timing, which is what makes "exactly once per frame" testable at all.

## Test plan
The suite is the deliverable; its own quality gates:
- **Self-verification**: each spec is confirmed to fail against a deliberately broken build (sync disabled, keyboard handler removed), so a spec that can never fail is caught.
- **Determinism**: 10 consecutive green runs required before a spec joins the required check.
- **Runtime**: the full suite <=15 minutes so it can run on every PR.
- **Traceability**: every spec names the E11-Q01 plan case or user-story scenario it automates.

## Security notes
Test-only code with synthetic fixtures; no credentials and no real account data. The fake WS server binds to localhost only and serves recorded fixture frames.

One control worth naming: the E2E harness route (`/__engine-harness`) exposes engine internals on `window` for assertions, and it must be **excluded from production builds** — a debug surface that ships is a genuine information-disclosure path. This is enforced by a build-time check and verified in **E11-X02**'s rule set, not left to reviewer vigilance.

## Accessibility notes
The keyboard-only specs are this suite's most valuable accessibility contribution: they assert that every chart capability is reachable without a pointer, which is `05-accessibility-standard.md` §3.1.6's requirement expressed as an executable test. A change that makes a feature drag-only or hover-only fails here, immediately, rather than being found in a manual pass months later.

The suite also asserts splitter keyboard resize, `Alt+T` table access and focus restoration on dialog close. Full WCAG conformance auditing (axe-core, screen readers, contrast) is **E11-Q05**.

## Performance notes
E2E timings are deliberately **not** used as performance gates — browser automation adds variance that swamps the signal, and a flaky perf gate is worse than none. Budgets are measured by the benchmark harness (E11-T06) and signed off in **E11-Q03**. The suite does assert that interactions complete within generous liveness timeouts, which catches a hang rather than a slowdown.

## Observability
Playwright HTML report, traces and videos published as CI artefacts on failure. Per-spec pass rate tracked over time so a spec degrading toward flakiness is visible before it becomes a nuisance and gets retried into meaninglessness.

## Definition of Done
- [ ] Test artefacts (plan, charters, scripts, suites) committed to the repo, not held in a personal document.
- [ ] Every scenario mapped to the Gherkin acceptance criterion or the user story it verifies, so coverage is traceable rather than asserted.
- [ ] Execution results recorded with pass/fail per scenario and evidence (logs, screenshots, recordings, benchmark artefacts) attached.
- [ ] Defects filed with reproduction steps, environment, severity and `priority/*`, linked to the E11 ticket they came from.
- [ ] Automated suites wired into CI at the correct stage and green; flaky tests quarantined with a ticket, never silently retried.
- [ ] Coverage contribution recorded against the package thresholds (>= 85 % engine, >= 80 % web).
- [ ] Sign-off comment posted by QA/SDET with pass/fail per scenario and any deviation stated explicitly.
- [ ] Test plan reviewed by the chart-engine lead so the black-box view and the implementation view are reconciled.

## Dependencies
- **E11-S09** — multi-pane and sync are a major part of the suite.
- **E11-Q01** — the plan this automates.
- **E11-S04**..**S07** — the interactions under test.
- Extended by **E12**, **E13**, **E14**, **E18**, **E21** for their own surfaces; feeds **E11-Q06**'s regression pack.

## Branch
`test/chart-engine-e2e` · 2 PRs (harness + interaction specs; multi-pane + sync + Electron runner), each <=400 LOC.

- `docs/plan/03-testing-strategy.md` — test pyramid, coverage floors, fixture conventions, flake policy

title: Establish and sign off the engine performance baselines against the budgets
body:
## Context
E11-T06 builds the benchmark harness and wires it as a required check. This ticket is the **human** half: running the full suite on the reference machine, comparing every number against the budgets in `06-performance-and-load-standard.md` and `26-chart-engine-design.md` §13, deciding whether the engine meets its contract, and recording a sign-off that the R1 PRR can rely on.

The distinction matters because a green CI check answers "is this worse than last week?" while a PRR needs "is this good enough to ship?" — and those are different questions. R1 exit criterion 1 requires "p95 <=16.6 ms with 100k bars + all R1 overlays on reference hardware in Electron", and somebody has to state, with evidence, whether that is true.

## Scope / Deliverables
- Full benchmark execution on the **reference machine** (`26-chart-engine-design.md` §1: Windows 11, Ryzen 7 / 8 cores, 32 GB, RTX 3060, 2560×1440 @125 %, pinned Electron build) in **both Chromium and Electron**.
- Scenarios: **B1** (pan, <=12 ms, <=8 draw calls), **B2** (zoom sweep, <=14 ms, <=6 LOD changes), **B5** (combined, <=16.7 ms, <=40 draw calls), **B6** (4 synced charts, <=16.7 ms aggregate, worker CPU <=70 % of one core), **B9** (cold init <=900 ms, atlas <=5 ms), **B10** (30-min soak, peak <=600 MB, growth <=5 %).
- **Budget #2 verification**: the 30 fps floor under the B6 worst case, with the degradation ladder active — measured, not inferred, since this is the number that decides whether the product is usable on a bad day.
- **Per-stage attribution** across the nine `06-performance-and-load-standard.md` §4.3 stages for B5, so the frame budget's internal allocation is evidenced and future regressions have a comparison point.
- **Memory verification**: measured usage vs the §7 model (~116 MB for the 100k-bar case), and the E11-S15 estimator's ±20 % accuracy claim independently confirmed.
- **Input-to-photon** (requirement R6: <=2 frames for pan/zoom/crosshair) measured with high-speed capture or the instrumented WS->pixel path.
- **Baseline commit**: the signed-off numbers become the stored baselines the CI gate compares against, with the runner's GPU, driver and Chromium versions recorded alongside them.
- **Sign-off document**: scenario, budget, measured value, verdict, and for anything not met, a named remediation ticket and owner.
- **Degradation-ladder verification**: forced over-budget conditions, confirming the ladder sheds in the specified order and never sheds a trading-critical overlay.

## Out of scope
- Building the harness — **E11-T06**.
- Backend API/WS load testing — E46 and the platform Epics.
- Optimisation work arising from findings — filed as tickets, executed by the engine team.
- Benchmarks for surfaces owned elsewhere (B3 footprint, B4 heatmap, B7 update storm, B8 drawings) — E18, E21, E17, E14, though their gates are registered in T06.

## Acceptance criteria
```gherkin
Scenario: Every budget has a measured verdict
  Given the budgets in 06-performance-and-load-standard.md and 26-chart-engine-design.md section 13
  When the sign-off document is complete
  Then each has a measured value and a pass or fail verdict on the reference machine
  And any fail carries a named remediation ticket with an owner, not a note to revisit later

Scenario: The 30 fps floor is measured under the worst case
  Given benchmark B6 with every R1 overlay enabled and the degradation ladder active
  When frame rate is sampled over the run
  Then the minimum sustained frame rate is recorded
  And the budget-2 verdict is based on that measurement rather than on the absence of complaints

Scenario: The ladder sheds in the specified order
  Given frames are forced over budget
  When the degradation ladder runs
  Then shedding follows the 4.4 order exactly
  And no order line, position line, SL or TP is shed at any rung

Scenario: The memory estimator's accuracy claim is independently verified
  Given the E11-S15 estimator predicts a footprint for a 30-day 1-minute load
  When the actual footprint is measured after loading
  Then the prediction is within 20 % of actual
  And the verification is performed by QA, not only by the estimator's own calibration test

Scenario: Baselines are committed with their environment recorded
  When the signed-off numbers become CI baselines
  Then the GPU model, driver version and Chromium build are recorded with them
  And a later driver upgrade invalidates the baselines explicitly instead of appearing as a mysterious regression

Scenario: Electron and Chromium are both reported
  When the suite is run
  Then results are reported separately for both runtimes
  And Electron is treated as the primary result, since it is the shipping shell
```

## Technical notes / design
**Method.** Three repetitions per scenario, median of p95 taken, per E11-T06's stability analysis. The machine is prepared identically each run: no other applications, power plan set to high performance, GPU at a settled thermal state (a benchmark run on a cold GPU and one on a hot GPU differ by more than the gate threshold).

**Why measure input-to-photon separately.** Frame time and latency are different properties: an engine can hold 16 ms frames while being three frames behind the input, and the chart would feel sluggish despite perfect benchmark numbers. R6's <=2 frames is measured either with a high-speed camera against a marker or via the instrumented WS->pixel path (E11-T07), and the method used is recorded.

**Per-stage attribution** is the part that pays off later: knowing that B5's 15 ms is 3 ms decode / 2 ms model / 4 ms batch / 5 ms GL / 1 ms present means a future regression can be attributed in minutes. Recording only the total makes every future investigation start from zero.

## Test plan
Verification of the measurements themselves:
- Repeatability: three runs per scenario with variance reported; a scenario whose variance exceeds 3 % is investigated before its number is trusted.
- Cross-check: engine-reported frame times cross-checked against Chrome DevTools tracing for at least one scenario, so a self-reported metric is validated against an independent one.
- The degradation-ladder verification is executed manually as well as automatically, because the specified *order* is easier to confirm by observation than by assertion.

## Security notes
Synthetic fixtures only; no real account data enters a benchmark. The sign-off document contains timing and memory data and is safe to attach to the PRR.

One note for the PRR record: benchmark results are gathered on the reference machine, which is not necessarily representative of every machine the terminal will run on. The sign-off states this limitation explicitly rather than implying universal coverage — the GPU matrix (**E11-Q07**) is the complementary evidence, and a PRR that reads only this document should know that.

## Accessibility notes
Benchmarks run with the **DOM mirror active**, so the accessibility layer's cost is inside the measured budget rather than excluded from it. This is stated in the sign-off because an engine benchmarked with accessibility disabled would produce numbers that do not describe the shipping product. The mirror's <=1 ms/frame budget is verified as part of the B5 stage attribution.

## Performance notes
This ticket *is* the performance verification. Budgets: **#1** (16.6 ms p95, 100k bars + 200-depth heatmap at 100 ms), **#2** (30 fps floor, worst case), **#14** (100 ms heatmap cadence — prepared here, gated in E21). Requirements **R6** (<=2 frames input-to-photon) and **R7** (<=600 MB per instance). Gates B1, B2, B5, B6, B9, B10. R1 exit criterion 1 depends on this sign-off.

## Observability
Sign-off document committed to `docs/plan/` and linked from the R1 PRR. Baselines committed to the repo with their environment metadata. Per-stage attribution published as a reference artefact so future regressions have a documented comparison point.

## Definition of Done

- [ ] Failures carry named remediation tickets with owners.

## Dependencies

title: Run a chaos charter for context loss, feed faults and resource pressure
body:
## Context
`00-planning-brief.md` lists chaos/failover tests among the non-negotiable SDLC requirements, and R1 exit criterion 8 is specific: a forced `WEBGL_lose_context` must restore a **fully correct scene within 2 s with zero data loss**.

The chart engine has an unusually rich set of ways to be disturbed that have nothing to do with its own logic: the GPU driver can reset, the browser can discard the context under memory pressure, the WS feed can gap or deliver out-of-order frames, the worker can be starved, the machine can sleep and wake. Each of these is a normal event over a long trading session, and each is invisible to unit tests. This charter exercises them deliberately.

## Scope / Deliverables
- **Context loss**: forced `WEBGL_lose_context` during idle, during a pan, during a data storm and during atlas generation; repeated loss (3× in 10 s); loss that fails to restore (asserting the SCR-048 path with auto-retry ×3 then manual retry).
- **Feed faults**: malformed binary frames; truncated frames; out-of-order sequence numbers; a sequence gap requiring resync; duplicate frames; `NaN` and `Infinity` prices; a declared length exceeding `maxBars`; a 60-second feed stall followed by a burst.
- **Resource pressure**: memory pressure to the 70 % threshold and beyond; GPU memory exhaustion; worker starvation (main thread blocked for 5 s); many charts opened and closed repeatedly (leak detection over 100 cycles).
- **Environment disturbance**: DPR change mid-pan; monitor disconnect; window minimise/restore; machine sleep/wake; tab backgrounded for 10 minutes then foregrounded (timers throttled, `rAF` stopped — a classic source of "the chart came back wrong").
- **Degraded paths**: WebGL2 unavailable at startup; WebGL2 lost permanently mid-session and falling back to `degraded-2d`; IndexedDB unavailable (private mode) during atlas caching.
- Each scenario asserts: **no crash, no silent wrongness, no data loss, a correct disclosure to the user, and full recovery** — with "no silent wrongness" being the one that matters most, since a chart that recovers into a subtly incorrect state is worse than one that visibly fails.
- Automated where deterministic (feed faults, context loss, pressure) in `packages/chart-engine/test/chaos`; manual charter for the environment disturbances that cannot be automated reliably.

## Out of scope
- Backend chaos (exchange 5xx, rate limits, WS disconnect at the server) — **E45** and the platform Epics; this charter covers the **client engine's** response to faults it receives.
- Performance measurement — **E11-Q03**.
- GPU/driver matrix coverage — **E11-Q07**.
- Security fuzzing as an adversarial exercise — **E11-X03** (this charter's malformed-frame cases overlap and feed it).

## Acceptance criteria
```gherkin
Scenario: Context loss restores a correct scene within the budget
  Given a chart with 100k bars, 3 panes and an active crosshair
  When WEBGL_lose_context is forced
  Then SCR-048 announces the loss through a role="alert" region
  And a fully correct scene is restored from the DataModel within 2 seconds with zero data loss
  And the viewport, crosshair position and pane ratios are exactly as they were

Scenario: Repeated context loss does not degrade into a broken state
  Given the context is lost three times within ten seconds
  Then each loss recovers correctly
  And after the third recovery the chart is fully functional with no leaked GPU resources

Scenario: A permanent loss falls back rather than failing
  Given the context cannot be restored after three attempts
  Then a manual retry and a link to renderer settings are offered
  And choosing the fallback moves the chart to degraded-2d with its capabilities disclosed

Scenario: Malformed frames are rejected without collateral damage
  Given a malformed, truncated or out-of-range frame arrives
  Then it is rejected with ENGINE_DECODE_ERROR
  And the existing scene continues rendering correctly, with no partial application of the bad frame

Scenario: A sequence gap resyncs rather than drawing wrong data
  Given frames arrive with a gap in the sequence
  Then the engine requests a resync rather than applying the later frames onto a stale model
  And the user is shown a stale indicator until the resync completes

Scenario: Backgrounding and restoring does not corrupt state
  Given the tab is backgrounded for ten minutes with a live feed
  When it is foregrounded
  Then the chart catches up to current data without a gap and without replaying ten minutes of animation
  And no duplicate or missing bars are present

Scenario: Repeated chart lifecycle leaks nothing
  Given a chart is created and disposed 100 times
  Then GPU memory and JS heap return to their starting level within 5 %
  And no worker, listener or observer is left alive
```

## Technical notes / design
**Forcing context loss.** The `WEBGL_lose_context` extension gives deterministic control, which is what makes this testable in CI rather than only by unplugging a monitor. Restoration correctness is asserted by comparing a **golden image** of the pre-loss scene with a post-restore capture — pixel comparison catches "restored but subtly wrong" in a way that state assertions do not.

**Leak detection.** 100 create/dispose cycles with `performance.measureUserAgentSpecificMemory()` sampled at the start and end. The threshold is 5 %, which tolerates allocator noise while catching a per-instance leak that would matter over a trading day.

**Background throttling.** Backgrounded tabs have `rAF` stopped and timers throttled to once per minute. The failure mode is an engine that, on foregrounding, either replays every missed frame (a visible animation storm) or holds a stale model believing it is current. Both are tested, because both have shipped in real products.

**Assertion discipline.** Every scenario asserts *correctness after recovery*, not merely "did not crash". A chaos test that only checks for exceptions passes happily while the chart shows yesterday's prices.

## Test plan
- Automated chaos suite in CI (nightly rather than per-PR — these are slow), with failures raised as P1.
- Manual charter for environment disturbances, executed once per release train with a session sheet.
- Golden-image comparison for every recovery scenario.
- Leak detection as a standalone long-running job.
- Findings filed with severity; anything producing silent wrongness is automatically **P0**, since it is the failure class the product can least afford.

## Security notes
This charter overlaps deliberately with **E11-X03**'s fuzzing: the malformed-frame, out-of-range and `NaN` cases are simultaneously robustness tests and security tests, since the same input that crashes a decoder is the one that corrupts memory in a less careful implementation. Findings are shared between the two tickets rather than duplicated.

The `maxBars` and `memoryBudgetMb` ceilings (E11-S15) are verified here under adversarial input, which is the control the STRIDE model relies on for denial of service. Data classification: synthetic fixtures only.

## Accessibility notes
Every disturbance must remain **announced and comprehensible**, because a screen-reader user has no visual cue that something went wrong:
- Context loss and restoration announce through `role="alert"` — once each, unthrottled.
- Stale and disconnected states are announced and are present in the DOM mirror, not only as a dimmed canvas.
- After recovery, keyboard focus and the data cursor position are preserved — a recovery that silently drops focus leaves a keyboard user stranded.
- The `degraded-2d` fallback discloses reduced capabilities in text.
These are asserted in the charter, not assumed from the implementation tickets.

## Performance notes
Recovery budgets: context restore <=2 s (R1 exit criterion 8); resync completes without exceeding the frame budget; the post-burst catch-up after a 60-second stall must not stall the UI thread. A recovery path that meets its correctness bar by blocking for 5 seconds fails this charter.

## Observability
Every scenario asserts the **correct engine error code** is emitted: `ENGINE_CONTEXT_LOST`, `ENGINE_CONTEXT_RESTORE_FAILED`, `ENGINE_NO_WEBGL2`, `ENGINE_MEMORY_PRESSURE`, `ENGINE_DECODE_ERROR`. Observability is treated as a testable requirement here — an error that recovers silently without telling anyone is a defect, because it makes the same problem in production undiagnosable.

## Definition of Done
- [ ] Test artefacts (plan, charters, scripts, suites) committed to the repo, not held in a personal document.
- [ ] Every scenario mapped to the Gherkin acceptance criterion or the user story it verifies, so coverage is traceable rather than asserted.
- [ ] Execution results recorded with pass/fail per scenario and evidence (logs, screenshots, recordings, benchmark artefacts) attached.
- [ ] Defects filed with reproduction steps, environment, severity and `priority/*`, linked to the E11 ticket they came from.
- [ ] Automated suites wired into CI at the correct stage and green; flaky tests quarantined with a ticket, never silently retried.
- [ ] Coverage contribution recorded against the package thresholds (>= 85 % engine, >= 80 % web).
- [ ] Sign-off comment posted by QA/SDET with pass/fail per scenario and any deviation stated explicitly.
- [ ] Test plan reviewed by the chart-engine lead so the black-box view and the implementation view are reconciled.

## Dependencies
- **E11-S02** — context-loss recovery is the central subject.
- **E11-T05** — the `degraded-2d` fallback path.
- **E11-T03**, **E11-S15** — decode validation and the memory ceilings under test.
- Feeds **E11-X03** (shared fuzzing findings) and **E11-Q06** (regression pack).

## Branch
`test/chart-engine-chaos` · automated suite plus the manual charter document.

## References
- `docs/plan/03-testing-strategy.md` — test pyramid, coverage floors, fixture conventions, flake policy
- `docs/plan/06-performance-and-load-standard.md` — budgets, measurement method, regression gate
- `docs/plan/05-accessibility-standard.md` — WCAG 2.2 AA target, canvas strategy, manual pass requirements
- `docs/plan/02-definition-of-ready-done.md` — QA sign-off gates per Kind

title: Audit the chart engine for WCAG 2.2 AA with axe-core and screen readers
body:
## Context
R1 exit criterion 9 requires that every chart is operable without a mouse, with **NVDA and VoiceOver passes signed off by the accessibility specialist**. `02-definition-of-ready-done.md` §8 makes a11y default-on for any UI surface with no "internal tool" exception, and `05-accessibility-standard.md` §6 identifies the canvas strategy as the highest-risk area in the product.

Automated tooling cannot verify most of what matters here. axe-core will confirm that a canvas has a `role` and that the table has headers; it cannot tell you whether the announcements make sense, whether the throttle cadence is tolerable at a 20 Hz tick rate, or whether the data table is genuinely usable as an equal-status alternative rather than technically conformant and practically miserable. That judgement requires a human using a screen reader, which is what this audit is.

**E11-D07** reviewed the design; this audits the built product against the same clauses.

## Scope / Deliverables
- **Automated**: axe-core zero violations on every R1 chart route — SCR-030, SCR-031, SCR-043, SCR-044, SCR-045, SCR-046, SCR-047, SCR-048, SCR-049 — wired as a required CI check.
- **Manual screen-reader passes**, each following a scripted task set and recorded:
  - **NVDA + Chrome** (Windows — the owner's platform, therefore primary).
  - **VoiceOver + Safari** (macOS).
  - **JAWS + Chrome** spot-check on the table and the live regions, where behaviour is known to diverge.
- **Task set** (the same tasks for each screen reader, so results are comparable): find the current price; navigate to a specific bar; read a bar's OHLCV; switch to log scale; open the data table and read three bars; sort the table by delta; move the crosshair and confirm the table follows; discover that the chart went stale; recover from a lost graphics context.
- **Keyboard-only audit**: every function reachable and operable, focus always visible, focus order logical, no traps, `Alt+T` and all documented hotkeys working, and no operation that requires hovering or dragging (§3.1.6).
- **Low-vision audit**: 200 % and 400 % browser zoom (WCAG 1.4.10 reflow); high-contrast theme; Windows High Contrast Mode; text spacing override (1.4.12).
- **Colour-independence audit**: every state and encoding checked under deuteranopia, protanopia and tritanopia simulation — feeding open item **O5** (colour-blind-safe palette), which is due at M8 and closes here.
- **Live-region behaviour audit**: cadence tolerable under a real 20 Hz feed; no flooding; discrete alerts announced once and in full; the "reduce announcements" toggle honoured.
- **Equal-status verification** of SCR-045 against the canvas, performed with a screen reader rather than by inspection.
- Findings triaged with WCAG criterion, severity and owner; **blocking findings gate the Epic's DoD**.

## Out of scope
- Design-stage review — **E11-D07** (already done; this audits the implementation against it).
- Accessibility of surfaces owned by other Epics (footprint cells, heatmap, drawings) — their own audits against this same standard.
- The design system's base components — E05.
- Remediation work — filed as tickets and executed by the owning teams.

## Acceptance criteria
```gherkin
Scenario: Automated checks are clean and enforced
  Given every R1 chart route
  When axe-core runs in CI
  Then zero violations are reported
  And the check is required, so a new violation blocks merge rather than being noticed later

Scenario: A screen-reader user can complete every task
  Given the scripted task set
  When it is executed with NVDA and again with VoiceOver
  Then every task is completed successfully
  And any task that cannot be completed is a blocking finding, not an observation

Scenario: The data table is genuinely equal status under a screen reader
  Given a screen-reader user reads a bar's values from the table
  When those values are compared with the canvas
  Then every value available visually is available in the table
  And the table is reachable from the panel header in at most the same number of keystrokes as any other primary chart control

Scenario: Announcements are usable at a real tick rate
  Given a live feed at 20 ticks per second
  When the ambient live region is listened to for two minutes
  Then announcements arrive at a tolerable cadence with the latest values
  And the screen reader is never flooded to the point of unusability

Scenario: The chart reflows at 400 percent zoom
  Given browser zoom at 400 percent
  When the chart and its chrome are inspected
  Then no content is lost and no two-dimensional scrolling is required for primary content
  And the data table's primary columns remain readable without horizontal scrolling

Scenario: Meaning survives without colour
  Given every state and encoding under three colour-blindness simulations
  Then each remains distinguishable
  And any encoding relying on colour alone is a blocking finding

Scenario: Recovery is perceivable without sight
  Given the graphics context is lost and restored
  When the session is observed with a screen reader
  Then both the loss and the recovery are announced once each, in full
  And focus and the data cursor position survive the recovery
```

## Technical notes / design
**Why three screen readers and not one.** NVDA, JAWS and VoiceOver differ substantially in how they handle live regions, virtualised tables and `role="img"` with dynamic labels — the three features this engine depends on most. Testing one and assuming the others is how products ship "accessible" charts that are silent in JAWS. NVDA is primary (owner's platform), VoiceOver full, JAWS spot-checked on the two features where divergence is known.

**Scripted, comparable tasks.** Each screen reader runs the same task list so results can be compared rather than merely collected. Each session is recorded with audio, which is the only practical way to review an announcement-cadence problem after the fact — "it felt like too much" is not a filable defect, and a recording is.

**Severity model.** Blocking = a task cannot be completed, or information is unavailable. Major = a task is completable but substantially harder than the pointer path. Minor = friction. Blocking findings gate the Epic DoD; major findings need an owner and a date before R1 PRR.

**O5 closure.** The colour-blindness simulation over the shipped palette is the M8 validation open item O5 has been waiting for; its result is recorded as an ADR amendment, closing the item.

## Test plan
- axe-core results per route, published as CI artefacts.
- Session recordings and per-task pass/fail per screen reader.
- Zoom, contrast and text-spacing screenshots.
- Colour-blindness simulation captures per state.
- Findings register with WCAG criterion, severity, owner and target ticket.
- Re-test after remediation, with results recorded — an audit without a re-test verifies nothing.

## Security notes
No security surface. One intersection worth recording: the DOM mirror surfaces market data as real DOM, and the audit confirms values are rendered as text rather than markup — the same control **E11-X01** models, verified here from the outside.

Session recordings capture screen content, so they are made against the **demo** environment with synthetic data and stored in the private QA drive.

## Accessibility notes
This ticket *is* the accessibility verification for E11, and its authority is R1 exit criterion 9 plus `05-accessibility-standard.md`. It audits all four layers of §6 as built:
- §6.1 DOM mirror — windowing, surrogate focus, alignment, sync with the canvas.
- §6.2 Live regions — cadence, politeness routing, region hygiene, the reduce-announcements toggle.
- §6.3 Table — equal status, column parity, sort/filter announcements, live patching without focus loss.
- §6.4 Canvas — `role="img"` with a current, updating label.
Plus §3.1.6 (no hover/drag-only), §4 (focus, target size, zoom) and §7 (reduced motion). Sign-off by the accessibility specialist is a **gate on the Epic's DoD**, not advisory.

## Performance notes
Two performance-adjacent findings the audit specifically looks for, because they are invisible to the perf harness: the announcement cadence must remain tolerable at full tick rate (a correctness problem for screen-reader users even though frame time is fine), and the DOM mirror must not degrade chart responsiveness when a screen reader is attached — AT attachment changes browser behaviour, and a chart that is smooth without NVDA and janky with it is a real and frequently-missed defect.

## Observability
Findings register committed to `docs/plan/`; axe-core results as CI artefacts; session recordings in the QA drive. `engine.a11y.desync_detected` and `engine.a11y.announcements_per_minute` are reviewed against the audit's observations, so the runtime counters are validated against human experience rather than trusted blindly.

## Definition of Done
- [ ] Test artefacts (plan, charters, scripts, suites) committed to the repo, not held in a personal document.
- [ ] Every scenario mapped to the Gherkin acceptance criterion or the user story it verifies, so coverage is traceable rather than asserted.
- [ ] Execution results recorded with pass/fail per scenario and evidence (logs, screenshots, recordings, benchmark artefacts) attached.
- [ ] Defects filed with reproduction steps, environment, severity and `priority/*`, linked to the E11 ticket they came from.
- [ ] Automated suites wired into CI at the correct stage and green; flaky tests quarantined with a ticket, never silently retried.
- [ ] Coverage contribution recorded against the package thresholds (>= 85 % engine, >= 80 % web).
- [ ] Sign-off comment posted by QA/SDET with pass/fail per scenario and any deviation stated explicitly.
- [ ] Test plan reviewed by the chart-engine lead so the black-box view and the implementation view are reconciled.
- [ ] axe-core zero violations on all R1 chart routes, wired as a required check.
- [ ] NVDA and VoiceOver passes completed with recordings and per-task results; JAWS spot-check completed.
- [ ] Zoom (200 %/400 %), high-contrast, Windows High Contrast Mode and text-spacing audits completed.
- [ ] Colour-blindness simulation completed and open item **O5** closed by an ADR amendment.
- [ ] All blocking findings resolved and re-tested; major findings owned with dates before R1 PRR.
- [ ] Signed off by the accessibility specialist (R1 exit criterion 9).

## Dependencies

title: Assemble the chart-engine regression pack and run the epic-level QA sign-off
body:
## Context
`02-definition-of-ready-done.md` §2.2 requires an **Epic-level** regression and exploratory pass, "not just child-ticket QA", and epic-level acceptance criteria "verified end-to-end, not just per-child". The reason is that an Epic can have every child green and still not work: each story was tested against its own acceptance criteria, and nobody sat down and used the chart for an hour.

E11 is also the Epic that six others build on, so this pack becomes the **standing regression suite** that E12, E13, E14, E15, E18 and E21 run against to prove they have not broken the chassis. Assembling it properly here is leverage; assembling it loosely means six Epics inherit a suite nobody trusts.

## Scope / Deliverables
- **Regression pack**: the durable, re-runnable subset of everything E11's QA produced — the E11-Q01 interaction cases, the E11-Q02 E2E suite, the E11-Q04 chaos scenarios, the E11-Q05 a11y checks and the E11-T08 golden images — assembled into one runnable suite with a single entry point and a documented runtime.
- **Epic-level acceptance verification**: each of the Epic's own Gherkin scenarios executed end-to-end and recorded — frame budget met and enforced; 30 fps floor under worst case; context loss recovering within 2 s with no data loss; the chart fully operable without a mouse; the engine package staying framework-free; graceful degradation without WebGL2.
- **Exploratory charters** (time-boxed, mission-stated, session-sheeted), aimed at the seams between stories where nobody's acceptance criteria live:
  1. *A trading session*: 60 minutes of realistic use on a live demo feed — switch symbols and intervals, pan history, scale modes, multi-pane, leave it running. Mission: find what degrades over time.
  2. *The awkward user*: deliberately hostile interaction — rapid mode switching, interrupted gestures, simultaneous keyboard and pointer input, resize during drag. Mission: find state corruption.
  3. *The keyboard-only trader*: complete a full session without touching the pointer. Mission: find the gaps between "technically operable" and "actually usable".
  4. *The long session*: 4 hours running with a live feed. Mission: find leaks, drift, stale state and recovery failures.
- **Cross-story seam testing**: theme change during a pan; LOD step-down while the data table is open; context loss during a sync propagation; memory pressure during atlas generation; DPR change mid-momentum.
- **Defect burn-down verification**: confirm zero open P0/P1 defects against E11 scope, as the Epic DoD requires.
- **QA sign-off document** for the Epic, feeding the R1 PRR evidence pack.

## Out of scope
- Writing new automated tests — this assembles and runs what exists; gaps found become tickets.
- Performance measurement — **E11-Q03** (its results are cited here, not re-derived).
- Accessibility auditing — **E11-Q05** (same).
- Other Epics' regression packs — they extend this one.

## Acceptance criteria
```gherkin
Scenario: Every epic-level acceptance criterion is verified end to end
  Given the six Gherkin scenarios in the E11 epic body
  When the sign-off is complete
  Then each has been executed end to end with evidence attached
  And none is signed off by pointing at a child ticket's test result

Scenario: The regression pack runs from one entry point
  Given the assembled pack
  When it is invoked
  Then interaction, E2E, chaos, a11y and golden-image suites all run
  And the total runtime is documented so downstream Epics can plan around it

Scenario: Exploratory charters are executed with recorded sessions
  Given the four charters
  When each is executed within its timebox
  Then a session sheet records what was covered, what was found and what was not covered
  And findings are filed with severity and owner

Scenario: The long session reveals no drift
  Given a four-hour session on a live demo feed
  When memory, frame time and correctness are checked at the end
  Then memory and frame time are within 5 percent of their starting values
  And no stale, desynced or silently incorrect state is present

Scenario: Cross-story seams behave
  Given a theme change during a pan, an LOD step-down with the table open, and a context loss during sync propagation
  When each is exercised
  Then the engine remains correct and recovers cleanly
  And any seam defect is filed against the specific pair of stories it sits between

Scenario: The epic cannot be signed off with open P0 or P1 defects
  Given the defect register for E11 scope
  When sign-off is attempted
  Then zero P0 and P1 defects are open
  And sign-off is withheld if any remain
```

## Technical notes / design
**Why exploratory charters matter most here.** Scripted tests verify what someone thought of in advance. E11's risk is concentrated in what nobody thought of — the interaction of LOD, memory pressure, theme changes, sync and live data over hours. Charters are time-boxed and mission-driven rather than step-scripted precisely so the tester follows the smell rather than the script.

**The long session is not optional and cannot be shortened.** Leaks, drift, texture-memory fragmentation and reconnect-loop bugs are invisible in a 10-minute run and obvious in a 4-hour one. A trading session is a full day; 4 hours is already a compromise.

**Pack composition principle**: fast checks first (unit, golden), then E2E, then chaos, then the manual charters. Downstream Epics run the automated portion per PR and the full pack per release train, and the entry point makes that split explicit rather than leaving each Epic to guess.

## Test plan
- Regression pack executed in full against the release candidate, with results recorded per suite.
- Epic-level acceptance scenarios executed with evidence attached per scenario.
- Four exploratory charters executed with session sheets.
- Defect register reviewed and confirmed clear of P0/P1.
- Pack runtime measured and documented.

## Security notes
Security findings arising from exploratory work are routed to **E11-X03** rather than filed as ordinary defects, per `02-definition-of-ready-done.md` §8's rule that anything with a security or safety implication is treated as `security`-labelled whether or not the label was applied at creation.

Sessions run against the **demo** environment; the four-hour session uses a demo feed, so no live account data appears in any recording or screenshot.

## Accessibility notes
The keyboard-only charter is a deliberate complement to **E11-Q05**'s conformance audit: conformance answers "does it meet the standard?", the charter answers "is it actually workable for a whole session?" — and a product can pass the first and fail the second. Its findings are as filable as any other.

The regression pack includes the axe-core checks and the keyboard traversal specs, so downstream Epics inherit accessibility regression protection automatically rather than having to remember to add it.

## Performance notes
Cites E11-Q03's measurements rather than re-deriving them, but the four-hour charter adds something the benchmark cannot: **drift over a realistic session**. B10's 30-minute soak catches fast leaks; a slow leak or gradual frame-time creep only shows over hours, and that is the specific thing this charter is looking for.

## Observability
Sign-off document committed and attached to the R1 PRR evidence pack. Session sheets and charter findings attached to the ticket. The regression pack's runtime and pass rate are tracked over time so downstream Epics can see whether the chassis suite is healthy.

## Definition of Done
- [ ] Test artefacts (plan, charters, scripts, suites) committed to the repo, not held in a personal document.
- [ ] Every scenario mapped to the Gherkin acceptance criterion or the user story it verifies, so coverage is traceable rather than asserted.
- [ ] Execution results recorded with pass/fail per scenario and evidence (logs, screenshots, recordings, benchmark artefacts) attached.
- [ ] Defects filed with reproduction steps, environment, severity and `priority/*`, linked to the E11 ticket they came from.
- [ ] Automated suites wired into CI at the correct stage and green; flaky tests quarantined with a ticket, never silently retried.
- [ ] Coverage contribution recorded against the package thresholds (>= 85 % engine, >= 80 % web).
- [ ] Sign-off comment posted by QA/SDET with pass/fail per scenario and any deviation stated explicitly.
- [ ] Test plan reviewed by the chart-engine lead so the black-box view and the implementation view are reconciled.
- [ ] Regression pack assembled with a single documented entry point and a measured runtime.
- [ ] All six epic-level acceptance scenarios verified end-to-end with evidence.
- [ ] All four exploratory charters executed with session sheets.
- [ ] Zero open P0/P1 defects against E11 scope.
- [ ] Epic QA sign-off document completed and attached to the R1 PRR evidence pack.

## Dependencies
- **E11-Q03**, **E11-Q04**, **E11-Q05** — their results and suites are assembled here.
- **E11-Q01**, **E11-Q02** — the interaction plan and E2E suite.
- **E11-T08** — golden images.
- Gates the **Epic DoD** and feeds the **R1 PRR**. Inherited by E12, E13, E14, E15, E18, E21.

## Branch
`test/chart-engine-regression-pack` · pack entry point and sign-off document committed.

- `docs/plan/06-performance-and-load-standard.md` — budgets, measurement method, regression gate
- `docs/plan/05-accessibility-standard.md` — WCAG 2.2 AA target, canvas strategy, manual pass requirements

title: Run an exploratory GPU, driver and runtime matrix charter for the engine
body:
## Context
The golden-image suite (E11-T08) runs on SwiftShader for determinism, which by construction means it **cannot catch driver-specific defects**. The benchmark suite (E11-T06) runs on one pinned reference machine, which means it cannot catch "works here, breaks there". Between them they leave a real gap, and risk **R8 Browser/GPU compat** lives in exactly that gap.

WebGL2 behaviour genuinely varies: Intel integrated graphics handle large textures differently from discrete NVIDIA; AMD drivers have historically differed on `fwidth` precision (which the SDF text shader depends on); WebView2 in Tauri behaves differently from Electron's Chromium (open item **O1**, ADR-0011); and vendor driver blocklists silently downgrade some machines to software rendering.

This charter is deliberately a **human exploratory activity** rather than an automated matrix: the failures being hunted are visual and subtle, and automating a matrix that nobody looks at would produce green checks and blurry text.

## Scope / Deliverables
- **GPU matrix**, each running the same scripted scenario set: NVIDIA discrete (the reference RTX 3060), AMD discrete, **Intel integrated** (the most commonly under-tested and most commonly broken), and a software-rendering fallback machine.
- **Runtime matrix**: Chromium (current stable), **Electron** (the pinned shipping build — primary), and **Tauri/WebView2**, closing out the measurement side of open item **O1**.
- **Driver variants**: current and one prior major driver version per vendor, since a regression introduced by a driver update is a support case that looks exactly like a product bug.
- **Scenario set** per combination: 100k-bar render and pan; SDF text at all size classes (the `fwidth` precision case); large-texture allocation (the heatmap ring's shape, even before E21 builds it); context loss and restore; `degraded-2d` forced via `renderer.forceProfile`; the full theme × density matrix at a glance.
- **Visual comparison** against the reference machine's captures, looking specifically for: blurry or misaligned text, hairline shimmer, colour-banding differences, missing or misplaced geometry, and texture-size failures.
- **Capability-probe verification**: the probe reports the correct profile on each machine, and a blocklisted GPU correctly falls back rather than attempting and failing.
- **Findings register** with the combination, the symptom, a capture, and whether it is a product defect, a driver bug to work around, or an accepted limitation.
- **Supported-configuration statement**: the concrete output — which GPU/driver/runtime combinations are supported, which are degraded, and which are unsupported, published in the docs so support has an answer.

## Out of scope
- macOS and Linux coverage beyond a smoke check — the owner's environment is Windows + Electron, and spreading thin across platforms nobody uses would cost coverage where it matters.
- Mobile/Android — out of scope for the whole plan (owner decision 2026-09-14).
- The Electron vs Tauri **decision** — ADR-0011, informed by these measurements but decided by the Architect.
- Performance baselines — **E11-Q03** (reference machine only, by design).

## Acceptance criteria
```gherkin
Scenario: Every matrix combination is exercised with the same scenarios
  Given the GPU, driver and runtime matrix
  When the charter completes
  Then each combination has run the full scenario set with results recorded
  And any combination that could not be tested is stated explicitly rather than silently omitted

Scenario: Text renders correctly on every GPU
  Given SDF text at all three size classes
  When it is compared against the reference capture on each GPU
  Then text is crisp and correctly positioned everywhere
  And any fwidth precision difference is identified with a workaround or an accepted limitation

Scenario: Intel integrated graphics is a first-class target
  Given an Intel integrated GPU
  When the full scenario set runs
  Then the engine either meets its targets or degrades correctly with disclosure
  And it never renders incorrectly without telling the user

Scenario: A blocklisted GPU falls back rather than failing
  Given a machine whose driver is on the browser's GPU blocklist
  When a chart is mounted
  Then the capability probe reports the reduced profile and degraded-2d is selected
  And the user is told what is reduced and why, and is never shown a blank canvas

Scenario: Open item O1 gets its measurements
  Given Tauri/WebView2 under the 100 ms-cadence update scenario
  When the results are recorded
  Then they are sufficient for ADR-0011 to be finalised
  And the recommendation is stated with its evidence

Scenario: The output is a supported-configuration statement
  When the charter completes
  Then a published statement names supported, degraded and unsupported combinations
  And support can answer a user's "does my machine work" question from it without asking engineering
```

## Technical notes / design
**Why exploratory rather than automated.** An automated cross-GPU matrix is expensive to build (a fleet of physical machines or a GPU-enabled cloud runner per vendor), and the defects it would catch are visual and contextual — "the text looks slightly soft on Intel" is not an assertion, it is an observation. A skilled tester with a reference capture and a side-by-side finds these in an afternoon. If a specific defect class recurs, *that* gets automated afterwards, which is the right order.

**Specific known-risk areas to probe hardest**, so the session is not a random walk:
- `fwidth` precision in the SDF shader (AMD historically differs) -> soft or fringed text.
- Maximum texture size and `texSubImage2D` upload performance (Intel integrated is the tight case) -> heatmap ring allocation failures.
- `OffscreenCanvas` availability and behaviour differences in WebView2 -> the whole worker architecture's assumption.
- Context-loss frequency under memory pressure (varies substantially by driver) -> recovery path exercised more often on some machines than others.
- High-DPI handling on mixed-DPI multi-monitor setups (the most common real-world configuration and the least tested).

**Capture discipline**: screenshots at fixed DPR and fixed viewport, so comparison against the reference is meaningful rather than approximate.

## Test plan
- Scripted scenario set executed per combination with captures.
- Side-by-side visual comparison against reference captures.
- Findings register with combination, symptom, capture and disposition.
- Recurring defect classes proposed for automation as follow-up tickets.
- Supported-configuration statement reviewed by the Architect and the support owner.

## Security notes
Synthetic fixtures only; no account data on test machines. Test machines are clean installs rather than personal machines, so a driver-level capture cannot inadvertently include unrelated content.

One security-adjacent finding class the charter watches for: a GPU or driver that silently produces **incorrect** rendering rather than failing is an integrity problem, not a cosmetic one — a chart drawing wrong prices is indistinguishable to the user from a data problem. Any such finding is escalated to P0 regardless of how narrow the affected configuration is.

## Accessibility notes
The `degraded-2d` path exercised here must retain **full accessibility** — the DOM mirror, data cursor, live regions and data table are main-thread DOM and are backend-independent. The charter verifies this on machines where the fallback is actually selected, rather than only on a reference machine where it is forced, since "forced fallback works" and "naturally selected fallback works" have diverged in practice before.

Windows High Contrast Mode is checked on the Windows machines, since it interacts with GPU rendering in ways the design-time review cannot predict.

## Performance notes
Performance on non-reference machines is recorded as **information, not as a gate** — the budgets are defined against the reference machine, and gating on an Intel integrated GPU would either be meaningless or would force the product down to the slowest machine's ceiling. What the charter does produce is the honest statement of what each class of machine delivers, which is what the supported-configuration statement needs and what support needs when a user asks why their laptop is slower.

## Observability
Findings register and supported-configuration statement committed to `docs/plan/`. The capability report (`ready` message) from each machine is captured, giving a real corpus of capability profiles rather than a theoretical one — useful later for interpreting a user's diagnostics snapshot.

## Definition of Done
- [ ] Test artefacts (plan, charters, scripts, suites) committed to the repo, not held in a personal document.
- [ ] Every scenario mapped to the Gherkin acceptance criterion or the user story it verifies, so coverage is traceable rather than asserted.
- [ ] Execution results recorded with pass/fail per scenario and evidence (logs, screenshots, recordings, benchmark artefacts) attached.
- [ ] Defects filed with reproduction steps, environment, severity and `priority/*`, linked to the E11 ticket they came from.

- [ ] Supported-configuration statement published and reviewed by the Architect.
- [ ] Open item **O1** measurements delivered to ADR-0011.
- [ ] Any silent-incorrect-rendering finding escalated to P0 regardless of configuration breadth.

title: Render via a dirty-flagged scene graph and budgeted frame scheduler
body:
## Context
The scene graph and the frame scheduler are the engine's heartbeat: every later feature is a node that gets traversed and a cost that has to fit in 16.6 ms. `26-chart-engine-design.md` §3.1 specifies a **deliberately shallow, fixed-depth** tree (`Chart -> Pane -> Layer -> Series`) "because depth costs traversal time per frame", and §3.2 specifies the loop with five binding rules: one rAF per chart instance, time-based animation, bounded work per frame, no allocation in the hot path, and render-on-demand parking.

The most important optimisation in the whole engine lives in §3.1's dirty-flag propagation: **a viewport change marks series `TRANSFORM`-dirty but not `DATA`-dirty**, so GPU buffers are reused and only uniforms change. Pan and zoom — the interactions a trader performs constantly — therefore cost almost nothing in buffer traffic. Getting this wrong is not a micro-optimisation miss; it is the difference between meeting budget #1 and not.

User value: this is the part of `US-CHART-001` and `US-CHART-006` that makes rendering smooth at all — the candle series itself ships in E12 against the seam built here.

## Scope / Deliverables
- `src/scene/` — node contract per §3.1: every node has `id`, `visible`, `zIndex`, `dirty` flags (`DATA | LAYOUT | STYLE | TRANSFORM`) and implements `update(frameCtx)` and `collect(batchBuilder)`. **Nodes never issue GL calls**; they append to batches so the backend can sort by program then texture.
- Fixed tree exactly as §3.1: `Chart -> TimeAxis (shared)` + `Pane[0..n]` where each pane holds `PriceAxis` and the ordered layers `background`, `heatmap`, `series[]`, `overlays`, `drawings`, `foreground`. Layer order is fixed and not configurable — z-order within a layer is `zIndex`.
- Dirty-flag propagation rules: data update -> affected series `DATA`; viewport change -> all series `TRANSFORM` (never `DATA`); theme change -> `STYLE`; pane resize -> `LAYOUT`. Flags clear after a successful collect.
- `src/scene/FrameScheduler.ts`: 16.7 ms budget, priority classification, **bounded 4 ms/frame data-mutation drain** with the remainder deferred, time-based (`dt`) animation integration, and render-on-demand parking (no rAF scheduled when nothing is dirty and no animation is running).
- `src/scene/BatchBuilder.ts`: per-layer draw batches, reused across frames, patched by sub-range rather than rebuilt; output is an ordered draw list sorted by program then texture.
- `src/scene/LayoutEngine.ts`: pane rects, axis gutters, height ratios (`Pane.setHeightRatio`), recomputed only on `LAYOUT` dirty.
- Object pooling for all per-frame structures (`frameCtx`, batch entries, pick results) so the hot path allocates nothing.
- LOD step-down hook: when the frame is over budget for **3 consecutive frames**, the scheduler drops one LOD level and logs it (the policy itself is E11-S12; the trigger lives here).

## Out of scope
- GL/context work and actual draw submission — E11-S02 consumes the ordered draw list.
- Viewport maths, momentum and autoscale — E11-S03/S04. The scheduler integrates animations; it does not know what a price is.
- Concrete series, overlay or drawing nodes — E12/E13/E14/E18/E19/E21. This story ships the node contract plus a test-only `NullSeries`.
- LOD *thresholds* and decimation algorithms — E11-S12.

## Acceptance criteria
```gherkin
Scenario: Panning reuses GPU buffers
  Given a chart with 100 000 bars and a static data feed
  When the viewport is panned continuously for 5 seconds
  Then every series is marked TRANSFORM-dirty and none is marked DATA-dirty
  And the count of bufferSubData calls recorded over the pan is zero

Scenario: The loop parks when there is nothing to do
  Given a mounted chart with no data arriving and no pointer interaction
  When 2 seconds elapse
  Then no requestAnimationFrame callback is scheduled after the last dirty frame
  And a single data message or pointer event resumes rendering on the next frame

Scenario: Data mutations are bounded, not dropped
  Given a burst of mutations that would cost 12 ms to apply in one frame
  When the scheduler drains the mutation queue
  Then at most 4 ms of mutations are applied in that frame and the rest are applied in following frames
  And no mutation is lost and ordering is preserved

Scenario: Animation is time-based, so dropped frames do not change the outcome
  Given a momentum animation is running
  When three frames are artificially dropped mid-animation
  Then the final resting viewport is identical (within 0.5 px) to an undropped run
  And no animation step uses a frame counter

Scenario: Sustained over-budget frames trigger a step-down
  Given the frame time exceeds 16.7 ms for 3 consecutive frames
  When the fourth frame is scheduled
  Then the scheduler requests one LOD level down and emits ENGINE_LOD_STEPDOWN with the stage timings
  And the step-down is visible in FrameStats.lodCandles

Scenario: The hot path allocates nothing
  Given the allocation-counter harness runs 600 frames of pan plus data updates
  When GC-triggering allocations in the frame path are counted
  Then the count is zero
```

## Technical notes / design
Traversal is a flat pre-order walk over a pre-linearised node array rebuilt only on `LAYOUT` dirty — pointer-chasing a tree every frame is exactly the cost §3.1 warns about.

`frameCtx` (pooled, one instance reused): `{ t, dt, viewport, theme, lod, budgetMsRemaining, stats }`. Nodes read it; they never mutate it except through `stats`.

Priority classification inside the budget, matching the stage allocation in `06-performance-and-load-standard.md` §4.3: input (<=1 ms) -> data drain (<=4 ms, hard-clamped) -> layout if dirty (<=2 ms) -> collect/cull (<=2 ms) -> GL submit -> present. When `budgetMsRemaining` goes negative, optional work (non-focused pane redraw, bubble clustering) is deferred to the next frame in the §4.4 order; **trading-critical overlays are never deferred** — that constraint is encoded as a `critical: true` flag on the node and asserted by a test.

Parking: `scheduleIfDirty()` is the only entry point that calls `requestAnimationFrame`. A `wake()` is called by the data port, the input router and the sync-group broadcaster. Double-scheduling is prevented by a single `frameHandle`.

Step-down hysteresis lives in E11-S12 (±15 % dead band); the scheduler only counts consecutive over-budget frames and raises the request.

## Test plan
- **Unit** (Vitest, `TestClock` replacing rAF per §14): dirty-flag propagation matrix (data/viewport/theme/resize -> expected flags on each node kind); flags clear after collect; parking and wake-up; budget clamping of the mutation drain; deferral order under budget pressure; `critical` nodes never deferred.
- **Property** (fast-check, 10 000 cases): for any random sequence of dirty marks and frames, no node is collected while clean, and every marked node is collected within one frame of being marked (or deferred with its flag retained — never silently cleared).
- **Determinism**: `TestClock` + `SeededRandom` (§14) — a 600-frame scripted session produces an identical draw-call trace across runs; asserted via the GL backend's trace recorder (structural assertions are cheaper and more stable than pixels).
- **Allocation**: allocation-counter test over 600 frames, zero GC-triggering allocations in the frame path.
- **Perf**: contributes the scheduler slice to B1/B5; scheduler overhead itself <=0.3 ms/frame with 3 panes and 12 nodes.
- Coverage >=85 %.

## Security notes
Data classification: **public market data only** — no PII, no credentials, no account identifiers. `packages/chart-engine` holds no secrets and performs no I/O (`CONSTITUTION.md` C-2.16), so spoofing/repudiation/elevation-of-privilege are out of band (they belong to E17's WS auth and E09's RBAC).

Residual STRIDE surface handled here (modelled in E11-X01): **Tampering** — typed arrays arriving from the decoder must be bounds- and value-validated before indexing (a hostile or corrupt frame must never become an out-of-bounds read or a `NaN` that poisons the viewport). **Denial of service** — every buffer has a hard ceiling (`maxBars`, `memoryBudgetMb`) so a malformed length field cannot allocate unboundedly.

Controls applied: no `eval`, no `Function` constructor, no shader source derived from data; worker constructed from a same-origin bundled URL so the page CSP needs no `worker-src blob:` widening; dependencies pinned and covered by npm audit / Dependabot. No security review label required beyond the epic-level E11-X03 sweep.

## Accessibility notes
The DOM-mirror sync (E11-S13) is a first-class stage in the frame, budgeted at <=1 ms per `06-performance-and-load-standard.md` §4.3, and it is **not** deferrable under budget pressure: §4.4 names "desyncing the DOM-mirror accessibility layer from what's visually rendered" as never acceptable. This story encodes that by marking the mirror-sync node `critical: true`, with a test asserting it is still executed on a frame where optional work is shed.

Reduced-motion: the scheduler exposes `prefersReducedMotion` in `frameCtx` so animated nodes can resolve instantly instead of easing; the honouring is per-node (E11-S04 for momentum).

## Performance notes
Directly owns budget #1 (<=16.6 ms p95) and budget #2 (30 fps floor). Stage instrumentation is added here so a regression is triaged by identifying the over-budget stage (`06-performance-and-load-standard.md` §9 profiling playbook) rather than re-profiling from scratch. Benchmarks touched: B1 (pan), B5 (combined), B6 (4 charts — validates the one-rAF-per-page rule holds when 4 instances share the worker).

## Observability
`Performance.mark()`/`measure()` spans at all nine §4.3 stage boundaries, emitted into `FrameStats` and surfaced by SCR-046. Stable codes: `ENGINE_FRAME_BUDGET_EXCEEDED` (with per-stage timings), `ENGINE_LOD_STEPDOWN` (with from/to level). Counters: `engine.frame.deferred_mutations`, `engine.frame.parked_ms`.

## Definition of Done
- [ ] Acceptance criteria verified by automated tests referencing each scenario by name.
- [ ] Coverage >= 85 % of new/changed lines in `packages/chart-engine` (>= 80 % for `apps/web` binding code); CI coverage gate green.
- [ ] `docs/plan/26-chart-engine-design.md` updated if the shipped behaviour diverged from the design; package README/TSDoc updated; changelog fragment added.
- [ ] axe-core CI green on touched chart routes (default-on: this package ships a UI surface).
- [ ] Benchmark run recorded against the affected budget in `06-performance-and-load-standard.md`; no regression beyond 5 % of baseline.
- [ ] SAST/SCA/secrets scan clean or findings triaged.
- [ ] QA sign-off comment with pass/fail per Gherkin scenario (E11-Q01 plan).
- [ ] Demoed at Sprint Review against staging (demo), or marked non-demoable infra-adjacent with Architect concurrence.
- [ ] PR(s) merged via the merge queue with 2 approvals including the `packages/chart-engine` code owner.

## Dependencies
- **E11-T01** — the facade, `Chart`/`Pane` types and the `RenderContext` shape nodes collect into.
- Blocks **E11-S02** (consumes the draw list), **E11-S09** (multi-pane), **E11-S12** (step-down policy), **E11-T04** (theme `STYLE` dirty path), and every series in E12+.

## Branch
`feat/chart-engine-core-scene-graph` · 3 PRs (node contract + traversal; scheduler + budget; batch builder + layout), each <=400 LOC. Pairing rule applies (risk R10 key-person): a second engineer reviews and can explain the dirty-flag rules.
